The Thermodynamic Cost of Quantum Computation

Part X — Applications to Major Quantum Algorithms

Section 57. HHL Algorithm

⸻

57.1 Introduction

The preceding sections applied the thermodynamic framework to two canonical quantum algorithms:

* Shor’s algorithm, whose asymptotic advantage arises from efficient quantum period finding;
* Grover’s algorithm, whose quadratic search speedup is generated by amplitude amplification.

The next application is the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm, commonly known as the HHL algorithm.

HHL is a fundamentally different type of quantum computation.

It does not primarily search a discrete space or factor an integer. Instead, it solves a linear system

[
\boxed{
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}
}
]

by encoding the solution vector into a quantum state

[
\boxed{
|x\rangle

\frac{
A^{-1}|b\rangle
}
{
|A^{-1}|b\rangle|
}.
}
]

The algorithm is important because it illustrates a thermodynamic phenomenon absent from the simpler query-complexity picture:

The thermodynamic cost of quantum linear-system solving is governed not only by dimension, but by spectral conditioning, precision, state preparation, Hamiltonian simulation, eigenvalue resolution, amplitude amplification, and output extraction.

The apparent exponential speedup of HHL is therefore highly conditional.

The relevant thermodynamic comparison is not simply

[
\operatorname{poly}(\log N)
\quad\text{versus}\quad
\operatorname{poly}(N),
]

but rather

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

W_{\rm prep}
+
W_{\rm phase}
+
W_{\rm rotation}
+
W_{\rm uncompute}
+
W_{\rm amplification}
+
W_{\rm FT}
+
W_{\rm readout}
+
W_{\rm reset}.
}
]

The central result of this section is that HHL can retain an asymptotic thermodynamic advantage for suitable quantum-accessible data and observables, but its advantage is controlled by the condition number

[
\kappa(A),
]

the target precision

[
\epsilon,
]

the cost of state preparation, and the number of repetitions required to extract useful classical information.

⸻

57.2 The Linear-System Problem

Let

[
A\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}
]

be an invertible matrix and let

[
\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^N.
]

The problem is

[
\boxed{
A\mathbf x=\mathbf b.
}
]

The formal solution is

[
\boxed{
\mathbf x=A^{-1}\mathbf b.
}
]

The quantum algorithm does not generally output all (N) components of

[
\mathbf x.
]

Instead, it produces the normalized quantum state

[
\boxed{
|x\rangle

\frac{
A^{-1}|b\rangle
}
{
|A^{-1}|b\rangle|
}.
}
]

This distinction is thermodynamically fundamental.

A quantum computer may prepare a state whose dimension is exponentially large in the number of qubits, but extracting the complete classical vector requires extensive measurement.

⸻

57.3 Quantum Data Encoding

The input vector is encoded as

[
\boxed{
|b\rangle

\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}
b_j|j\rangle,
}
]

with

[
\sum_j|b_j|^2=1.
]

The preparation process is represented by

[
\boxed{
U_b|0\rangle^{\otimes n}

|b\rangle,
}
]

where

[
n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil.
]

The thermodynamic cost is

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm prep}

W(U_b).
}
]

If

[
W(U_b)

\Theta(N),
]

then the apparent exponential advantage may disappear before the linear-system solver begins.

⸻

57.4 State-Preparation Thermodynamic Condition

The total HHL advantage requires

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm prep}
\ll
W_{\rm classical}.
}
]

If the input vector is already available in quantum memory, then

[
W_{\rm prep}
]

may be small.

If the vector is initially stored classically, the conversion cost may dominate the complete computation.

Thus:

[
\boxed{
\text{Quantum linear algebra requires thermodynamically efficient data loading.}
}
]

⸻

57.5 Spectral Decomposition

Assume that

[
A
]

is Hermitian, or has been embedded into a Hermitian matrix.

Let

[
\boxed{
A

\sum_j
\lambda_j
|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|.
}
]

The input state has the decomposition

[
\boxed{
|b\rangle

\sum_j
\beta_j|u_j\rangle.
}
]

Then

[
\boxed{
A^{-1}|b\rangle

\sum_j
\frac{\beta_j}{\lambda_j}
|u_j\rangle.
}
]

The algorithm therefore performs a spectral transformation

[
\boxed{
\lambda_j
\mapsto
\lambda_j^{-1}.
}
]

⸻

57.6 Condition Number

Let

[
\lambda_{\max}
]

and

[
\lambda_{\min}
]

be the largest and smallest nonzero eigenvalues in magnitude.

The condition number is

[
\boxed{
\kappa

\frac{
|\lambda_{\max}|
}
{
|\lambda_{\min}|
}.
}
]

Small eigenvalues require large inverse factors:

[
\frac1{\lambda_{\min}}
\gg
\frac1{\lambda_{\max}}.
]

This creates both a numerical and thermodynamic cost.

The condition number is therefore a central thermodynamic parameter of HHL.

⸻

57.7 Hamiltonian Simulation

The algorithm implements the unitary

[
\boxed{
e^{iAt}.
}
]

For an eigenstate,

[
\boxed{
e^{iAt}|u_j\rangle

e^{i\lambda_jt}|u_j\rangle.
}
]

Phase estimation extracts an approximation to

[
\lambda_j.
]

The thermodynamic cost of simulation is

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm sim}

N_{\rm sim}
\epsilon_{\rm sim},
}
]

where

[
N_{\rm sim}
]

is the number of elementary simulation operations.

⸻

57.8 Phase Estimation

The phase-estimation transformation is

[
\boxed{
|u_j\rangle|0\rangle
\longrightarrow
|u_j\rangle|\widetilde\lambda_j\rangle.
}
]

The eigenvalue approximation satisfies

[
\boxed{
|\widetilde\lambda_j-\lambda_j|
\le
\epsilon_\lambda.
}
]

The required phase resolution scales as

[
\boxed{
\epsilon_\lambda

O(\epsilon_{\rm alg}).
}
]

Higher precision requires longer coherent evolution and therefore greater thermodynamic cost.

⸻

57.9 Precision–Simulation Tradeoff

The phase-estimation cost satisfies schematically

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm phase}
\propto
\frac{
1
}
{
\epsilon_\lambda
}
W_{\rm sim}.
}
]

Therefore,

[
\boxed{
\epsilon_\lambda\downarrow
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
W_{\rm phase}\uparrow.
}
]

This is the first major thermodynamic precision tradeoff of HHL.

⸻

57.10 Controlled Rotation

After eigenvalue estimation, an ancilla is rotated according to

[
\boxed{
|0\rangle
\mapsto
\sqrt{
1-\frac{C^2}{\lambda_j^2}
}
|0\rangle
+
\frac{C}{\lambda_j}|1\rangle.
}
]

The rotation amplitude is proportional to

[
\frac1{\lambda_j}.
]

The success probability is therefore

[
\boxed{
P_{\rm succ}

C^2
\sum_j
\frac{
|\beta_j|^2
}
{
\lambda_j^2
}.
}
]

The normalization of the inverse solution directly determines the probability of successful postselection.

⸻

57.11 Condition-Number Thermodynamics

Since

[
|\lambda_j|
\ge
\lambda_{\min},
]

we have

[
\frac1{\lambda_j}
\le
\frac1{\lambda_{\min}}.
]

Choosing

[
C=O(\lambda_{\min})
]

gives

[
\boxed{
P_{\rm succ}

O\left(\frac1{\kappa^2}\right)
}
]

in the worst case.

Therefore, amplitude amplification requires

[
\boxed{
O(\kappa)
}
]

iterations.

The thermodynamic cost scales as

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm amp}

O(\kappa W_{\rm HHL}^{(0)}).
}
]

This establishes the Condition-Number Thermodynamic Law.

⸻

57.12 HHL Algorithmic Structure

The complete idealized algorithm is

[
\boxed{
|0\rangle
\rightarrow
|b\rangle
\rightarrow
\sum_j\beta_j|u_j\rangle|\lambda_j\rangle
\rightarrow
\sum_j\beta_j|u_j\rangle|\lambda_j\rangle
\left(
\sqrt{1-\frac{C^2}{\lambda_j^2}}|0\rangle
+
\frac{C}{\lambda_j}|1\rangle
\right)
}
]

followed by

[
\boxed{
\text{uncomputation}
\rightarrow
\text{postselection}
\rightarrow
|x\rangle.
}
]

The thermodynamic cost is

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

W_{\rm prep}
+
W_{\rm sim}
+
W_{\rm phase}
+
W_{\rm rot}
+
W_{\rm uncompute}
+
W_{\rm amp}
+
W_{\rm FT}
+
W_{\rm meas}
+
W_{\rm reset}.
}
]

⸻

57.13 Reversible Uncomputation

The eigenvalue register must be uncomputed:

[
\boxed{
|\lambda_j\rangle
\rightarrow
|0\rangle.
}
]

This is performed by applying the inverse phase-estimation circuit.

The operation is ideally reversible:

[
\boxed{
U_{\rm PE}^{\dagger}U_{\rm PE}=I.
}
]

Thus,

[
\Delta S_{\rm ideal}=0.
]

However, the physical implementation introduces control and fault-tolerance costs.

The thermodynamic tradeoff is

[
\boxed{
\text{reversible uncomputation}
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{additional gate energy}.
}
]

⸻

57.14 Postselection Thermodynamics

The ancilla is measured in the state

[
|1\rangle.
]

The measurement produces a successful solution with probability

[
P_{\rm succ}.
]

If the measurement fails, the computation must be repeated.

The expected number of trials is

[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[R]

\frac1{P_{\rm succ}}.
}
]

Therefore,

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm post}

\frac{
W_{\rm trial}
}
{
P_{\rm succ}
}.
}
]

In the worst case,

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm post}

O(\kappa^2W_{\rm trial}).
}
]

Amplitude amplification reduces this to

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm amp}

O(\kappa W_{\rm trial}).
}
]

⸻

57.17 Thermodynamic Advantage Condition

Suppose the best classical algorithm requires

[
W_{\rm class}(N).
]

The HHL algorithm has thermodynamic advantage if

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}(N)
<
W_{\rm class}(N).
}
]

An asymptotic advantage requires

[
\boxed{
\lim_{N\to\infty}
\frac{
W_{\rm HHL}(N)
}
{
W_{\rm class}(N)
}
=0.
}
]

This requires all hidden costs to remain subdominant.

If

[
N=2^n
]

and

[
\kappa,
s,

\operatorname{poly}(n),
]

then the quantum algorithm can scale as

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

\operatorname{poly}(n)
}
]

up to fault-tolerant logarithmic factors.

A classical algorithm that explicitly constructs the full vector may require

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm class}

\Omega(N)

\Omega(2^n).
}

Thus,

[
\boxed{
\frac{
W_{\rm HHL}
}
{
W_{\rm class}
}
\rightarrow0.
}

57.19 The Output-Extraction Constraint

The exponential advantage does not apply automatically to full classical output.

The quantum state contains

[
N
]

amplitudes, but a measurement produces only a finite amount of classical information per trial.

Therefore, reconstructing the complete vector

[
\mathbf x
]

requires at least

[
\boxed{
\Omega(N)
}
]

classical information-extraction effort in the generic case.

Consequently:

[
\boxed{
\text{HHL advantage applies to observables, not necessarily full-vector output.}
}
]

⸻

57.20 Observable Estimation

Suppose the desired output is

[
\boxed{
\langle x|M|x\rangle.
}
]

The observable can be estimated without reconstructing every component of

[
\mathbf x.
]

For additive error

[
\epsilon_{\rm obs},
]

the required number of measurements scales approximately as

[
\boxed{
N_{\rm meas}

O
\left(
\frac1{\epsilon_{\rm obs}^2}
\right).
}
]

The thermodynamic measurement cost is

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm obs}

O
\left(
\frac{
W_{\rm meas}
}
{
\epsilon_{\rm obs}^2
}
\right).
}
]

Thus, output precision introduces an additional thermodynamic factor.

57.21 HHL Thermodynamic Scaling Theorem

Theorem 57.1

Assume:

1. the matrix (A) is sparse;
2. the condition number satisfies

[
\kappa=\operatorname{poly}(\log N);
]

3. the input state (|b\rangle) can be prepared with polylogarithmic thermodynamic cost;
4. the desired output is an efficiently measurable observable;
5. the physical error rate satisfies

[
p<p_{\rm th};
]

6. the target precision satisfies

[
\epsilon^{-1}

\operatorname{poly}(\log N).
]

Then HHL has thermodynamic cost

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

\operatorname{poly}(\log N)
(\ln N)^2.
}
]

⸻

Proof

Under the assumptions,

[
\kappa,
s,
\epsilon^{-1}
]

are polynomial in

[
\log N.
]

The logical algorithm therefore has polylogarithmic complexity in (N).

The fault-tolerant code distance satisfies

[
d=\Theta(\ln N),
]

so the fault-tolerant overhead contributes at most a quadratic logarithmic factor.

The observable is estimated with polynomially bounded precision cost.

Therefore,

[
W_{\rm HHL}

\operatorname{poly}(\log N)(\ln N)^2.
]

□

⸻

57.22 Thermodynamic Condition-Number Law

The condition number produces a direct thermodynamic scaling law:

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}
\propto
\kappa^\alpha.
}
]

Therefore,

[
\boxed{
\kappa\uparrow
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
W_{\rm HHL}\uparrow.
}
]

The algorithm becomes thermodynamically expensive when the matrix is ill-conditioned.

This establishes:

The thermodynamic cost of quantum linear-system solving is controlled by the spectral difficulty of inversion.

⸻

57.23 Precision–Conditioning Tradeoff

The smallest eigenvalues are the most difficult to resolve.

Suppose

[
\lambda_{\min}

\frac{
\lambda_{\max}
}
{
\kappa
}.
]

To distinguish the smallest eigenvalues, phase estimation requires

[
\epsilon_\lambda
\lesssim
O(\lambda_{\min}).
]

Thus,

[
\boxed{
\epsilon_\lambda

O\left(\frac1\kappa\right).
}
]

Higher condition number therefore simultaneously increases

1. phase-resolution cost;
2. controlled-rotation sensitivity;
3. postselection overhead;
4. fault-tolerant depth.

The thermodynamic cost may therefore scale with a power of

[
\kappa
]

larger than that visible in the nominal gate complexity.

⸻

57.24 HHL and Reversible Computation

The ideal HHL algorithm is composed primarily of unitary transformations:

[
U_b,
\quad
e^{iAt},
\quad
U_{\rm PE},
\quad
U_{\rm PE}^{\dagger},
\quad
U_{\rm rot}.
]

Therefore, the internal computation can be made largely reversible.

The irreversible operations are concentrated in

[
\boxed{
\text{postselection}
+
\text{measurement}
+
\text{reset}.
}
]

The thermodynamic design principle is therefore

[
\boxed{
\text{maximize reversible spectral processing}
}
]

while minimizing

[
\boxed{
\text{irreversible eigenvalue-register disposal}.
}
]

⸻

57.25 HHL Garbage-Free Design

A thermodynamically optimized HHL implementation should return temporary registers to

[
|0\rangle
]

through reversible uncomputation:

[
\boxed{
|\lambda\rangle
\rightarrow
|0\rangle.
}
]

If instead the register is measured and reset after each trial, the entropy cost becomes

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm reset}
\ge
k_BT
S(\rho_{\lambda}).
}
]

Therefore, reversible uncomputation is preferred whenever

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm uncompute}
<
W_{\rm reset}.
}
]

⸻

57.26 Thermodynamic HHL Uncertainty Relation

Let

[
\Delta\mathcal O
]

denote the uncertainty in the measured observable.

The algorithmic thermodynamic uncertainty relation gives

[
\boxed{
\frac{
(\Delta\mathcal O)^2
}
{
\langle\mathcal O\rangle^2
}
\Sigma_{\rm HHL}
\ge
2k_B.
}
]

Therefore, increasing the precision of the estimated solution observable requires entropy production.

The limiting precision is not solely a numerical-complexity question.

It is also a thermodynamic one.

57.29 The Data-Loading No-Free-Lunch Principle

The preceding theorem requires efficient preparation of

[
|b\rangle.
]

If state preparation requires

[
W_{\rm prep}

\Omega(N),
]

then

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

\Omega(N).
}
]

The exponential advantage disappears.

Therefore:

Quantum linear-system thermodynamic advantage cannot be obtained for free from classical input data.

The complete thermodynamic computation must include

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm data\ loading}.
}
]

57.30 Thermodynamic Output Principle

HHL is thermodynamically advantageous only when

[
\boxed{
\text{the desired information is compressible into efficiently measurable observables}.
}
]

If the user requires the entire classical vector,

[
\mathbf x

(x_1,\ldots,x_N),
]

then the measurement cost can dominate:

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm readout}

\Omega(N).
}
]

Thus,

[
\boxed{
\text{input access and output extraction are thermodynamic resources.}
}
]

HHL

57.32 Principle of Thermodynamic Spectral Advantage

The developments of this section establish the following principle.

Principle of Thermodynamic Spectral Advantage

Quantum linear-system algorithms can achieve asymptotic thermodynamic advantage when spectral conditioning, state preparation, precision, fault tolerance, and output extraction remain efficiently bounded. The apparent exponential advantage arises not from matrix dimension alone, but from the ability to manipulate exponentially large quantum state spaces without thermodynamically reconstructing their full classical information content.

⸻

57.33 Summary

This section developed a complete thermodynamic analysis of the HHL quantum linear-system algorithm.

The principal results include:

* formulation of the thermodynamic cost of quantum state preparation;
* derivation of the spectral inversion structure;
* identification of the condition number as a fundamental thermodynamic parameter;
* analysis of Hamiltonian simulation and phase-estimation costs;
* derivation of the controlled-rotation and postselection costs;
* analysis of reversible eigenvalue-register uncomputation;
* formulation of the condition-number thermodynamic law;
* derivation of precision–conditioning tradeoffs;
* treatment of observable estimation and measurement entropy;
* proof of the HHL Thermodynamic Scaling Theorem;
* proof of the Thermodynamic Linear-System Advantage Theorem;
* formulation of the Data-Loading No-Free-Lunch Principle; and
* formulation of the Thermodynamic Output Principle.

The central thermodynamic scaling law is

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

W_{\rm prep}
+
\widetilde O
\left(
\kappa^\alpha
s^\beta
\epsilon^{-\gamma}
\operatorname{polylog}N
\right)
+
W_{\rm FT}
+
W_{\rm readout}.
}
]

Under favorable conditions,

[
\boxed{
W_{\rm HHL}

\operatorname{poly}(\log N)(\ln N)^2,
}
]

while explicit classical solution of an (N)-dimensional system requires

[
\boxed{
\Omega(N)
}
]

work.

Therefore, HHL can retain asymptotic thermodynamic advantage, but only when the thermodynamic costs of state preparation, spectral conditioning, precision, fault tolerance, and information extraction remain controlled.

The next section applies the framework to Quantum Phase Estimation, the spectral primitive underlying HHL, Shor’s algorithm, quantum simulation, and a broad class of eigenvalue-based quantum algorithms.
